content:
On August 9 this year, the Hong Kong Observatory recorded the highest temperature in its history since records began in 1884 — 36.9°C — and in Sheung Shui it exceeded 39.8°C in the early afternoon. In this sweltering heat, I took shelter in a long, narrow house, leaving only a crack in the window for air. In extreme heat, the hot air really does rush indoors. So I shut the balcony door and the living room windows completely. I live on a mid-floor flat between two small hills; apart from noon, the sun is blocked from every direction. Even without air conditioning, three ceiling fans whirred and stirred up cool breezes. In a Hong Kong-style heatwave, one must count one's blessings.

Under record-breaking temperatures, I stayed home to do the laundry. Shortly after 1 p.m., I washed two large bedsheets with duvet covers, four pairs of jeans and a big pile of T-shirts. Two hours later, I turned the bedsheets and covers over to sun-dry on the other side. In the end, past 6 p.m., I held the warm fabric — as if just taken from a commercial dryer at a laundromat — and laid it on the bed. It felt as though I had not experienced such naturally sun-dried, clean laundry in half a century. I ought to have been worrying about my friends under the fierce sun; only by washing the clothes bundle by bundle could I offset, just a little, the loathsomeness of that blazing sun.

August has become a nightmare. I do not know how many more visits will be needed to break free from that repeating summer of partings. In a night's dream, I proudly twirled my mother forward as I walked, saying: "My little mummy." I held her tightly with joy. Then, ahead, I saw a mysterious woman draped in a long, deep maroon cloak. Subconsciously, I did not want to see her face clearly, but the dream's camera kept zooming in on her features — she was a strange woman I did not recognise. Until I woke, the feeling of triumphant exhilaration surged up, and what I recalled was: I had dreamed of my mother again.

On the evening of August 10, 2020, our whole family sang hymns, kissed mother's forehead and bade her farewell — it was a full stop. Yet letting go is a lesson hard to learn in a lifetime. Not letting go is a hidden wound. Six years on, there are still countless small regrets, and in my mind I keep replaying the days that led up to that day six years ago.

The regret and reluctance of parting — sooner or later, at any age — appear at different stages of life. In a writing class, a student wrote about her late maternal grandmother. It was a piece of recollection, mourning or remorse. When she was very small, she had resented living with her grandmother in the countryside. During the day, with the energy of a little imp, she bickered with her grandmother; when her grandmother pinched her ear, she struck back, letting the old woman feel the pain too. Then, through a crack in the door, the little child saw her doddering grandmother secretly wiping away tears. That very night, the girl fell ill with a fever, walked blankly to her grandmother and said: "I feel awful."

To feel awful means to feel unwell — that is how a child perceives illness. She had a high fever, her whole body was burning. Without a word, her grandmother found clean clothes and changed her, then immediately carried her on her back to the hospital to wait. That smell of medicated oil, once despised, carried her hazily to the hospital. Before long, somehow, the scent faded. The little girl sat alone near the reception desk, and then some adults asked her: "Where are your family?" As she spoke, she began to cry, until the smell of medicated oil drifted close again, and she waited calmly to see the doctor for an injection and medicine.

Back home, the medicated oil scent lingered as usual, but seemed to have lost its pungency. From the kitchen came the sound of meat being chopped on a board, and the fragrance of rice porridge wafting from a hot pot. The essence of life in this world needs no further explanation — it is as simple and clear as that.

I wonder: today, when I am ill, who will be the one cooking porridge for me?

When I was small, it was mostly my father, sometimes my mother, who would have the patience to hand-chop beef and make porridge for me. This was a sick-day menu, and only I would eat it. Sometimes, after seeing the doctor, I would pre-order this kind of meat congee: "I want the beef and spring onion porridge." That was the privilege of being ill. Now, no one makes this particular dish for me anymore, and even when I am sick, I will never again eat this beef porridge.

"These days when you're sick, just order from FoodPanda," a friend said. Some friends cook plain porridge or fish congee for their wives. "Sometimes I make minced pork congee too." "I chop it by hand, not with a blender." "Just a few minutes of chopping and it's done." Because a pot of porridge makes one feel cherished.

"In a lifetime, not many people will cook porridge for you when you are ill. After growing up, the most likely scenario is that you will cook it for others. Most people have been through this. Whatever your thoughts, bid a proper farewell, speak from the heart. Those who read it will feel comforted on your behalf." I told the student. She looked at me, and a glint flickered in her eyes.

A piece of writing about grandmother can bring comfort. My father, my mother, my grandmother... these are stories we naturally know how to write.

The student is not simply a good writer. She seized on the medicated oil as the central thread, and around it conveyed the genuine feelings between her and her closest family. She may not have been the one who loved her grandmother most, but that time together, arranged by fate, means she can never forget all that her grandmother did for her, nor fail to understand that people grow through such unwitting processes. In the end, she turned in a deeply moving and truly "heart-wrenching" piece.

The medicated oil went from being hated, to dependable, to shameful, to cherished memory. It turns out that on the girl's first day of primary school, classmates laughed at her for smelling of medicated oil and called her a country bumpkin. She ran home crying and angrily ordered her grandmother — "my po" — to scrub every single piece of clothing from top to bottom with heavy doses of washing powder. The grandmother, clutching the laundry, wept. From when the girl was eight months old, her grandmother had raised her; now that she had grown and started school, encountering the wider world, the little girl had become almost a different person, and had hurt her grandmother's heart. After returning to live with her mother, one day her grandmother had already developed dementia (Alzheimer's disease). The girl went back with her mother to visit, only to discover she was no longer "recognised".

"You can't be my granddaughter. She doesn't like talking to me," the old grandmother told the girl.

Life is both real and cruel. Have I ever been this cruel to my own mother? Perhaps not. Or perhaps I have, just like her. Family members sometimes hurt one another. The point is whether, afterwards, we come to understand love more deeply.
